title: Death of a Partner
outcomes: Explain how accounting for the death of a partner differs from retirement.
Apply Section 37 of the Indian Partnership Act to compute the estate's claim when settlement is delayed.
List what the legal representatives are entitled to and liable for, and close the deceased partner's account to the Executor's Account.
Estimate profit up to the date of death on the time and turnover bases and record it through a Profit and Loss Suspense Account.
Account for joint life and separate life policies on death and for payment of the executor in instalments.

meta.exam_tip: Death questions usually ask only for the deceased partner's capital account and the executor's account — show every computation as a working note so that step marks survive an arithmetic slip.

concepts.title: Death of a partner — like retirement, with a few extra steps
body: On the death of a partner the surviving partners usually continue the business (reconstitution). The accounting is close to retirement: revalue assets and liabilities, distribute reserves, adjust goodwill and deal with the joint life policy — all in the old ratio up to the date of death, with goodwill borne by the gaining partners.

Three things are special to death: (1) death can happen on any day, so the deceased partner's share of profit from the last balance sheet date to the date of death must be estimated; (2) a joint life policy actually matures and the full policy amount is received; (3) the amount due is paid to the legal representatives (executors), not to the partner, and the deceased's capital is transferred to an Executor's Account.
concepts.analogy: Retirement is a planned exit with notice; death is a sudden exit, so the accountant must also work out "profit till today" on an estimate.
concepts.work: Families of a deceased partner often depend on the settlement. Accountants must be fair, prompt and able to explain every figure to people who are not accountants.

concepts.title: Section 37: share of subsequent profits or 6% interest
body: Provision: under Section 37 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, if a partner dies or leaves the firm in any other way and the others carry on the business with the firm's property without settling his account, then — unless there is a contract to the contrary — he or his estate may choose either (a) the share of profits made since he ceased to be a partner that is attributable to the use of his share of the firm's property, or (b) interest at 6% per annum on his share of the property.
The choice is with the outgoing partner or his representatives, and they need not decide until the profit figure is known.

Exception: if the deed gives the continuing partners an option to buy the outgoing partner's interest and they exercise it properly, no further share of profits is due. If they do not comply with its terms in all material respects, Section 37 applies.
In exam questions the share of profit "attributable to the use of his share of property" is usually taken as profit × his capital ÷ total capital.
concepts.analogy: If someone keeps using your share of a shop without paying you, the law lets you take either your fair share of what the shop earned or simple interest — whichever is better for you.
concepts.work: Delays in settling a deceased partner's dues are common (probate, disputes). The firm should provide for the Section 37 liability every year until settlement, or it understates its liabilities.

concepts.title: What the legal representatives receive — and what they bear
body: Entitled to: balance of the deceased's capital (and current) account; interest on capital up to the date of death if the deed allows; share of goodwill; share of reserves and undistributed profits; share of revaluation profit; share of profit up to the date of death; share of the joint life policy (or separate policies).
Liable for: drawings; interest on drawings; share of revaluation loss; share of any loss up to the date of death.

After these adjustments the balance of the capital account is transferred to the Executor's Account (Deceased Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To His Executor's A/c). Payment follows the agreement — lump sum or instalments; if there is no agreement, the representatives are entitled to interest at 6% p.a. from the date of death till payment (or the Section 37 option).
concepts.analogy: A closing statement for the family: every right of the partner is added, every advance he took is subtracted.
concepts.work: Accountants usually prepare this statement in a simple "amount due to the estate" format so the family's lawyer can verify it quickly.

concepts.title: Profit up to the date of death and the Profit and Loss Suspense Account
body: Time basis: assume profit accrues evenly through the year. Profit to death = last year's (or average) profit × months up to death ÷ 12; deceased's share = that × his ratio.
Turnover (sales) basis: assume the same profit margin as last year. Rate = last year's profit ÷ last year's sales; profit to death = sales up to death × rate.

Because the year's accounts are not closed yet, the share is credited through a Profit and Loss Suspense Account: P&L Suspense A/c Dr. To Deceased Partner's Capital A/c. At year end the suspense account is closed to the Profit and Loss (Appropriation) Account, so the surviving partners finally bear it out of the year's profit.
concepts.analogy: Paying a share of a season's earnings half-way through the season: either pro-rata by time, or by how many tickets have been sold so far.
concepts.work: The basis must come from the deed. If the business is seasonal, time basis can be badly unfair — accountants often recommend the turnover basis in such deeds.

concepts.title: Joint life policy on death
body: On death the insurer pays the full policy amount to the firm. Bank A/c Dr. To Joint Life Policy A/c.
Method 1 (premium charged to P&L; policy not in books): the whole amount received is a gain, credited to ALL partners including the deceased in the old ratio.
Method 2 (policy at surrender value): only the amount received in excess of the book value is a gain, credited in the old ratio.
Method 3 (policy and JLP Reserve at surrender value): as in method 2, and the JLP Reserve is also transferred to all partners in the old ratio.
concepts.analogy: A group insurance cheque arrives after one member's death: it is shared among all members (the deceased's share going to his family) in the agreed proportion.
concepts.work: The JLP claim is often the main source of cash to pay the executor. Accountants follow up the claim papers with the insurer alongside the settlement.

concepts.title: Separate life policies on death
body: Where each partner's life is insured separately (premium charged to P&L), only the deceased partner's policy pays out — the full policy amount. The surviving partners' policies continue, but their surrender values are counted too.
The total of (deceased's policy amount + surrender values of the other policies) is credited to all partners in the profit sharing ratio — the deceased's share to his Executor's Account.

blocks.text: Example: partners 3:2; policy on the deceased ₹1,00,000; surrender value of the other partner's policy ₹20,000. Total ₹1,20,000 → executor ₹48,000 (2/5) if the deceased held 2/5.

concepts.analogy: One umbrella paid out a big claim, the others still have a resale value: the family gets its share of everything.
concepts.work: The accountant obtains a surrender value certificate for each surviving partner's policy as at the date of death.

concepts.title: Paying the deceased partner's share
body: The executor may be paid at once (Executor's A/c Dr. To Bank A/c), or the balance may be kept in the firm and paid in instalments with interest, exactly like a retiring partner's loan.

The basic difference from retirement is the finalisation of the amount: besides goodwill and revaluation (done as on retirement), the executor gets the share of profit up to the date of death and the share of the actual JLP proceeds.
concepts.analogy: Settling an estate: the amount is fixed first, then the family and the firm agree on a payment plan.
concepts.work: Interest on the executor's balance is a charge against profit; the firm must also deduct and deposit tax at source on such interest where the law requires — a practical point many small firms forget.

jobs.title: Preparing the estate's claim after a partner's death
jobs.role: Accountant of a family partnership firm
jobs.situation: A senior partner has died mid-year. His children (the legal heirs) ask the firm how much is due and when it will be paid. The surviving partners want to continue the business.
steps: Read the deed: basis for profit up to death, goodwill, interest on capital, and payment terms.
Lodge the joint life policy claim with the insurer and track it.
Compute profit up to death (time or turnover basis), revaluation, reserves, goodwill and JLP share; deduct drawings.
Transfer the balance to the Executor's Account and agree a payment plan; if payment is delayed without agreement, provide for interest at 6% p.a. or the Section 37 option.
Obtain the legal representative documents (will/probate or succession certificate) before paying out.
jobs.takeaway: Death settlements combine accounting with law and sensitivity: correct figures, the right payee, and clear explanations.
jobs.think: The business is seasonal — 70% of sales happen between October and March. The partner died on 30 September. Which basis is fairer for profit to death?
jobs.answer: The turnover basis, because time basis would credit half the year's profit although much less than half was actually earned by 30 September.

jobs.title: Section 37 claim during a delayed settlement
jobs.role: Article assistant reviewing a firm's year-end accounts
jobs.situation: A partner died eight months ago; his estate has not been paid because of a family dispute, and the firm is using the money.
steps: Check whether the deed excludes Section 37 or gives the partners a purchase option that was exercised.
If not, compute both options (share of profit attributable to his share of property, and 6% interest) for the period since death.
Recommend providing for the higher amount, since the representatives may choose it.
jobs.takeaway: Until the estate is settled, the firm carries a liability that grows with time — and the law lets the estate pick the better option.

mcqs.q: Under Section 37 of the Indian Partnership Act, if the business is continued without settling a deceased partner's account, his estate may claim, at its option, interest on his share of the property at:
mcqs.explain: Section 37 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 protects the estate of a deceased (or outgoing) partner when the surviving partners carry on the business with the firm's property without settling his account. The estate may claim, at its option, either the share of profits earned by using his share of property, or interest at 6% per annum on that share. The trap is 12% — a common rate in deeds, not the statutory one. In practice: executors usually compare both options before choosing.
mcqs.topic: Right of Outgoing Partner in Certain Cases to Share Subsequent Profits

mcqs.q: A partner with a 1/5 share dies 3 months after the year end. Last year's profit was ₹2,40,000. On the time basis his share of profit to death is:
mcqs.explain: Time basis: assume profit accrues evenly through the year. Profit for 3 months on last year's basis = 2,40,000 × 3/12 = ₹60,000. His 1/5 share = 60,000 × 1/5 = ₹12,000. The trap ₹60,000 is the firm's profit for the period, not his share; ₹48,000 gives him 1/5 of the full year. In practice: since final accounts are not ready on the date of death, firms use last year's profit or sales as a reasonable estimate.
mcqs.topic: Amount Payable to Legal Representatives of Dead Partner

mcqs.q: The deceased partner's share of profit up to the date of death is credited to his capital account by debiting:
options: Profit and Loss Appropriation Account of last year
Surviving partners in the gaining ratio
mcqs.explain: When a partner dies mid-year, the current year's accounts are not yet ready. His estimated share of profit is credited to his capital by debiting a Profit and Loss Suspense Account, a temporary account closed when the year's accounts are prepared. The trap is debiting surviving partners in the gaining ratio — that is the treatment for goodwill, not for profit earned while he was alive. In practice: firms use this suspense account to settle an estate quickly without waiting for year-end.
mcqs.topic: Amount Payable to Legal Representatives of Dead Partner

mcqs.q: Last year a firm earned ₹1,50,000 on sales of ₹10,00,000. Sales up to the date of a partner's death were ₹4,00,000. Profit to the date of death on the turnover basis is:
mcqs.explain: Turnover basis: assume profit bears the same ratio to sales as last year. Last year's margin = 1,50,000 ÷ 10,00,000 = 15%. Profit up to death = 4,00,000 × 15% = ₹60,000. The trap ₹40,000 uses a 10% margin instead of 15%; ₹1,50,000 is last year's full profit. In practice: for seasonal businesses such as crackers or school uniforms, the turnover basis gives a fairer estimate than time basis.
mcqs.topic: Amount Payable to Legal Representatives of Dead Partner

mcqs.q: Premiums on a joint life policy of ₹5,00,000 have always been charged to P&L. On the death of a partner the amount received is:
options: Credited to all partners including the deceased in the old ratio
Credited only to the deceased partner
Credited to the surviving partners in the gaining ratio
Credited to Profit and Loss Suspense
mcqs.explain: When premiums are expensed, the policy is not in the books, so the whole ₹5,00,000 received on death is a gain of the firm. It is credited to all partners, including the deceased, in their old profit-sharing ratio; the deceased's share goes to his estate. The trap 'only the deceased partner' treats the JLP like personal insurance, but the firm paid the premiums and owns the policy. In practice: firms buy JLPs precisely to have funds to pay a deceased partner's estate.
mcqs.topic: Special Transactions in Case of Death: Joint Life Policy

mcqs.q: JLP ₹3,00,000 is carried at its surrender value of ₹45,000. On a partner's death the gain credited to partners is:
mcqs.explain: The JLP is already in the books at its surrender value of ₹45,000. On death the insurer pays the full ₹3,00,000. The gain is the excess over book value: 3,00,000 − 45,000 = ₹2,55,000, credited to all partners in the old ratio. The trap ₹3,00,000 double-counts the ₹45,000 already included in the partners' capitals through the asset. In practice: the accountant closes the JLP account and records the insurer's claim receipt in the bank.
mcqs.topic: Special Transactions in Case of Death: Joint Life Policy

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT payable to the legal representatives of a deceased partner?
options: His share of profit earned by the firm after final settlement of accounts
His share of profit up to the date of death
mcqs.explain: The estate is entitled to the deceased's capital plus his share of goodwill, revaluation profit, reserves and profit up to death. Once the account is finally settled, the estate has no further connection with the firm, so profits earned after settlement belong only to the surviving partners. The trap is 'share of goodwill' — goodwill is paid because the survivors gain his share of future profits. In practice: settlement deeds include a release clause confirming the estate's claims end on payment.
mcqs.topic: Amount Payable to Legal Representatives of Dead Partner

mcqs.q: A, B and C share 3:1:1 and hold separate policies (premiums charged to P&L): A — surrender value ₹12,000; B — surrender value ₹10,000; C — policy amount ₹60,000. C dies. The amount credited to C's executor in respect of the policies is:
mcqs.explain: Separate life policies are firm assets. On C's death, his policy yields ₹60,000; the other policies are valued at surrender value: 12,000 + 10,000. Total = ₹82,000. C's share = 1/5 × 82,000 = ₹16,400. The trap ₹60,000 gives C's estate the whole of his own policy, ignoring that the firm owns all policies and they are shared in profit ratio. In practice: insurance advisers often suggest separate policies so that the firm's funds match each partner's risk.
mcqs.topic: Special Transactions in Case of Death: Separate Life Policy

mcqs.q: Once all adjustments are made, the balance of a deceased partner's capital account is transferred to:
mcqs.explain: After all adjustments, the balance in the deceased partner's capital account is the amount the firm owes his estate. It is transferred to his Executor's (legal representative's) Account, shown as a liability until paid. The trap is transferring it to surviving partners' capitals, which would absorb his money into their accounts. In practice: firms pay the executor or legal heir only after obtaining a succession certificate or probate, as banks and auditors require proof.
mcqs.topic: Special Transactions in Case of Death: Payment of Deceased Partner’s Share

mcqs.q: A deceased partner's share in the firm's property is ₹1,80,000. The business is continued for 4 months without settlement and the estate opts for interest. The amount is:
mcqs.explain: The estate chose interest under Section 37, at 6% per annum on the deceased's share of property for the period the business continued unsettled: 1,80,000 × 6% × 4/12 = ₹3,600. The trap ₹10,800 applies 6% for a full year, and ₹7,200 uses 12%. In practice: executors weigh this 6% interest against the share of profits actually earned, and choose whichever is higher.
mcqs.topic: Right of Outgoing Partner in Certain Cases to Share Subsequent Profits

mcqs.q: The Profit and Loss Suspense Account debited on a partner's death is closed at the end of the year by transfer to:
mcqs.explain: The Profit and Loss Suspense Account is temporary: it holds the deceased's share of estimated profit until the year's accounts are prepared. At year-end it is closed by transfer to the Profit and Loss (Appropriation) Account, so the year's total profit bears that share. The trap is transferring it to the executor — the executor was already credited through the capital account. In practice: auditors check that the suspense account carries no balance in the year-end balance sheet.
mcqs.topic: Amount Payable to Legal Representatives of Dead Partner

mcqs.q: The deed gives surviving partners an option to purchase a deceased partner's share, and they duly exercise it. Under Section 37 the estate is:
options: Not entitled to any further share of profits
Entitled to a share of all future profits
mcqs.explain: The proviso to Section 37 says that if the deed gives surviving partners an option to buy the deceased partner's share and they duly exercise it, the estate is not entitled to any further share of profits. The trap '6% interest anyway' ignores that the option, once properly exercised, ends the estate's claim to profits or interest. In practice: well-drafted deeds include buy-out clauses so that survivors can settle the estate on fixed terms.
mcqs.topic: Right of Outgoing Partner in Certain Cases to Share Subsequent Profits

questions.q: Arjun, Bhavna and Chetan were equal partners. Chetan died on 31 August 2026. After all adjustments the capitals were Arjun ₹1,00,000, Bhavna ₹1,50,000 and Chetan ₹2,50,000. Arjun and Bhavna continued the business with the firm's assets and paid Chetan's executor only on 30 November 2026. Profit for September to November was ₹48,000. The deed is silent. Advise the executor, with reference to the law, and compute the amount.

model.provision: Section 37 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932: where the surviving partners carry on the business with the firm's property without final settlement with the estate of a deceased partner, the estate may, unless otherwise agreed, claim at its option either the share of profits since death attributable to the use of the deceased's share of the property, or interest at 6% p.a. on that share. No further share is due if a purchase option in the deed is duly exercised.
model.facts: Chetan's share in the firm's property is ₹2,50,000 out of ₹5,00,000. The business was carried on for 3 months without settlement and earned ₹48,000. The deed is silent, so no purchase option exists.
model.analysis: Option (a): 48,000 × 2,50,000 ÷ 5,00,000 = ₹24,000. Option (b): 2,50,000 × 6% × 3/12 = ₹3,750. The executor may wait until the profit is known before choosing.
model.conclusion: The executor should choose the share of profits, ₹24,000, in addition to the amount already due on Chetan's capital account.

remarks: Many candidates compute interest for a full year instead of the three months of delay.
Answers that give only one option score half marks at best — the essence of Section 37 is the choice.
mistakes: Taking the profit share in the profit sharing ratio (1/3) instead of the share in property.
Quoting the interest rate as 12% or 9%.
tips: Use Provision → Facts → Analysis → Conclusion even in an accounting paper when law is asked.
Always compute both options and say which one the estate will choose.

The deed provides: (i) interest on capital at 9% p.a.; (ii) profit up to death on the basis of sales — last year's sales ₹30,00,000 and profit ₹4,50,000; sales from 1 April to 31 October 2026 were ₹20,00,000; (iii) goodwill valued at ₹2,50,000, not to be shown in the books; Dinesh and Fatima will share 3:2 in future. General Reserve stood at ₹40,000; revaluation resulted in a loss of ₹15,000. The firm's joint life policy of ₹2,50,000 appeared at ₹45,000 with a JLP Reserve of equal amount; the policy amount was received. ₹2,19,500 was paid to the executor on 31 October; the balance carries interest at 6% p.a. Prepare Esha's Capital Account and her Executor's Account up to 31 March 2027.

mistakes: Using the time basis when the deed says sales basis.
Debiting goodwill to the surviving partners in the old ratio 2:1.
Forgetting to debit the revaluation loss.
tips: Do every computation as a numbered working note first, then post them into the capital account.

summary: Death = retirement adjustments + profit to date of death + actual JLP proceeds + payment to the executor.
Section 37: if business continues with firm property without settlement, the estate chooses share of profits attributable to its share of property or 6% p.a. interest.
Profit to death: time basis (months/12) or turnover basis (sales to date × last year's margin); P&L Suspense Dr, Deceased's Capital Cr.
JLP on death: full amount received; gain over book value credited to all partners in old ratio; JLP reserve also distributed.
Separate policies: deceased's policy amount + surrender values of the others, shared in profit ratio.
Balance of capital → Executor's A/c; paid at once or in instalments with interest.
remember: P&L Suspense is closed to P&L Appropriation at year end.
Without agreement, the executor gets 6% p.a. from death till payment.
traps: Don't give the executor profits earned after the account is settled.
Don't double count the JLP book value — credit only the excess, plus any reserve.
Don't use time basis if the deed says sales basis.

viva.q: What right does Section 37 of the Partnership Act give to the estate of a deceased partner?
viva.model: If the surviving partners carry on the business with the firm's property without settling the deceased partner's account, his estate can choose either the share of profits made since his death that can be traced to the use of his share in the property, or interest at six per cent per annum on his share. This applies unless there is a contract to the contrary, and no further profit is due if a purchase option in the deed is duly exercised.

viva.q: How is a deceased partner's share of profit up to the date of death calculated?

His share is then credited to his capital account by debiting the Profit and Loss Suspense Account.

viva.q: What happens to the joint life policy on the death of a partner when the premium has been charged to profit and loss account?
viva.model: The firm receives the full policy amount from the insurer. Since the policy was not shown in the books, the whole amount is a gain, and it is credited to all the partners including the deceased partner in their old profit sharing ratio. The deceased partner's share goes to his executor.

viva.q: What is the main difference between accounting for the death of a partner and for retirement?
viva.model: The adjustments are mostly the same — revaluation, reserves, goodwill and life policy. The differences are that on death the partner's share of profit from the last balance sheet date to the date of death has to be estimated through a profit and loss suspense account, the joint life policy actually matures so the full amount is received instead of the surrender value, and the amount due is paid to his executor or legal representatives.

cases.title: Pia's estate
cases.case: Om, Pia and Raj share profits 2:1:1; accounts close on 31 March. Pia died on 31 August 2026. Her capital (after reserves and revaluation) was ₹1,20,000. Profit up to death is to be taken on the time basis using last year's profit of ₹1,80,000. The firm's joint life policy of ₹4,00,000 was carried at its surrender value of ₹60,000, and the policy amount was received. Pia's estate was paid only four months after her death, with no agreement on interest; assume the estate opts for interest on the full amount due.

mcqs.q: Pia's share of profit up to the date of death is:
mcqs.explain: Pia died on 31 August, 5 months after the year began on 1 April. Time basis: firm's profit to death = 1,80,000 × 5/12 = ₹75,000. Pia's 1/4 share = 75,000 × 1/4 = ₹18,750. The trap ₹75,000 is the firm's profit for 5 months, not her share; ₹15,000 uses 4 months. In practice: since annual accounts are not ready on death, firms estimate her share from last year's profit and credit it to her capital.
mcqs.topic: Amount Payable to Legal Representatives of Dead Partner

mcqs.q: Pia's share of the joint life policy credited to her capital is:
mcqs.explain: The JLP was carried at ₹60,000, already reflected in partners' capitals. The insurer paid ₹4,00,000, so the gain is 4,00,000 − 60,000 = ₹3,40,000, shared in the old ratio. Pia's 1/4 = ₹85,000. The trap ₹1,00,000 takes 1/4 of the full policy amount, double-counting the surrender value already in her capital. In practice: firms buy JLPs so that such claims fund the payment to a deceased partner's family.
mcqs.topic: Special Transactions in Case of Death: Joint Life Policy

mcqs.q: The total amount transferred to Pia's executor is:
mcqs.explain: Amount due = capital 1,20,000 + share of profit to death 18,750 + share of JLP gain 85,000 = ₹2,23,750, transferred to her executor's account. The trap ₹2,38,750 uses ₹1,00,000 as her JLP share, double-counting the surrender value. In practice: the firm records a liability to the executor and pays it after the legal heirs produce succession documents.
mcqs.topic: Special Transactions in Case of Death: Payment of Deceased Partner’s Share

mcqs.q: Interest payable to the estate for the four months of delay is:
mcqs.explain: Since the estate was paid four months late without any agreement, Section 37 lets it claim 6% per annum on the amount due: 2,23,750 × 6% × 4/12 = ₹4,475. The trap ₹13,425 applies 6% for a full year; ₹2,238 covers only 2 months. In practice: delays in settling a deceased partner's estate cost the firm interest, so firms keep funds such as JLP proceeds ready.
